etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Latin discriminatus, past participle of discriminare (“to divide, separate, distinguish”), from discrimen (“a space between, division, separation, distinction”), from discerno (“to divide, separate, distinguish, discern”); see discern, discreet, discrete. Compare crime.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, construed with against) To make decisions harmful to (a person or group) based on prejudice.
(intransitive, construed with against, uncommon) To infringe upon (a person's rights) in a prejudicial manner.

quote.citation: 1977 January 19, Anita Bryant, quotee, “Bias Against Homosexuals Is Outlawed in Miami”, in New York Times, page 14:
quote.text: The ordinance condones immorality and discriminates against my children's rights to grow up in a healthy, decent community.

quote.citation: 2012 August 28, “Federal court finds discrimination in new Texas voting maps”, in CBS News‎[1]:
quote.text: There's also expected to be a ruling out of Washington over Texas' efforts to impose a restrictive new voter law that many minority groups allege discriminates against their right to vote.

quote.citation: 2019 June 20, “Illinois Reproductive Health Act FAQ”, in ACLU Illinois‎[2], archived from the original on 6 July 2019:
quote.text: Under the RHA, a person can sue the State of Illinois or local governments like cities and counties if they improperly deny, interfere with, or discriminate against the person’s fundamental rights to make their own reproductive health decisions.

definitions.definition: To treat or affect differently, depending on differences in traits.
(transitive) To set apart as being different; to mark as different; to separate from another by discerning differences; to distinguish.

quote.citation: 1670-7, Isaac Barrow, “Sermon XX: Against rash Censuring and Judging”, in The Theological Works, volume 1, published 1818, page 448:
quote.text: To discriminate the goats from the sheep.

quote.citation: 1782–1785, William Cowper, “(please specify the page)”, in The Task, a Poem, […], London:  […]  J[oseph] Johnson;  […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Still stranger much, that when at length mankind Had reach'd the sinewy firmness of their youth, And could discriminate and argue well On subjects more mysterious

definitions.definition: Having the difference marked; distinguished by certain tokens.

quote.citation: 1627 (indicated as 1626), Francis [Bacon], “IX. Century.”, in Sylua Syluarum: Or A Naturall Historie. In Ten Centuries. […], London:  […]  William Rawley […]; [p]rinted by J[ohn] H[aviland] for William Lee […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Nevertheless it is certain, that oisters, and cockles, and mussels, which move not, have no discriminate sex
